newTable.text: Table E.3: Distinguishing forms of positive thought and the evidence about them Study Design and comparison What the finding supports—and leaves open Oettingen and Mayer (2002), Study 3 Measured expectations and fantasies among 117 students, then followed preparation and course-grade improvement over six weeks Expectations and fantasies had different relationships with later effort and performance; the observational design does not isolate the effect of increasing confidence Kappes and Oettingen (2011), Study 3 Randomly assigned 49 students to ideal-positive imagery about the coming week or thoughts about it without an instructed emotional tone; 40 completed follow-up Ideal-positive imagery reduced immediate reported energy and reported accomplishment one week later; self-reports and incomplete follow-up limit the conclusion Oettingen et al. (2001) Four experiments compared imagining a desired future and then present obstacles—mental contrasting—with other ways of thinking about the future or present Contrasting made commitment more dependent on expectations of success; the studies did not establish that those expectations were accurate
